question: The three large autonomous communities in the Spanish hinterland are those hardest hit by unsuitable and high-impact deployment of renewable energy. At the end of 2024, Castilla y León had 7 300 MW installed, Aragón 5 700 MW and Castilla-La Mancha 5 100 MW, representing 57 % of Spain’s 32 000 MW of wind energy capacity. The wind farms cover an area measuring 256 000 km² (51 % of the total) that is home to 6.

8 million residents (14 % of the Spanish population). The same three autonomous communities also had more than 13 000 MW of installed photovoltaic capacity. Virtually all the renewable energy in these territories is controlled by large companies, many of which are financed by public money from the EU and Spain.

In 2024, the total number of energy communities installed in Spain was less than 400, with fewer than 75 in Aragón, Castilla-La Mancha and Castilla y León. The installed capacity from renewable energy in energy communities makes up less than 1 % of the total. In light of the above: 1.

Does the Commission not consider that rural energy communities urgently need to be promoted and financed in order to provide energy sovereignty and self-consumption in rural regions such as Aragón, Castilla-La Mancha and Castilla y León?
Does the Commission not believe that energy communities will strengthen rural communities and be effective in curbing depopulation?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.12.2025) The Commission considers that rural areas are a fertile ground for the development of energy communities. The EU framework calls for enabling frameworks for energy communities1, including tools to facilitate access to finance and information.

How to tailor the implementation is however at the discretion of the Member States, in accordance with national specificities and policy preferences. The Commission has promoted the development of rural energy communities through the Rural Energy Communities Advisory Hub2 providing direct technical assistance to 28 rural energy communities.

With the newly established Citizen Energy Advisory Hub, the Commission will continue to support rural communities3. In parallel, the Energy Communities Facility4 provides grant support for energy communities to develop business plans.

As announced in the Affordable Energy Action Plan5, the Commission will furthermore adopt a Citizens Energy Package to further enhance the participation of citizens in the energy transition. Qualitative evidence suggests that energy communities can indeed help to curb depopulation in rural areas6 and to ensure that benefits stay local7.

In line with the objectives of the Longterm Vision for the EU’s rural areas8, the Commission is supporting the set up of energy communities in rural areas through the Citizen Energy Advisory Hub, the Energy Communities Facility, the LEADER and Smart villages approaches and wider CommunityLed Local Development (CLLD), if selected in local development strategies9, as well as LIFE Clean Energy Transition (CET) programme.
For example, JALON10 LIFE project, aims to empower inhabitants of rural areas by creating a regional energy community model and addressing the needs of the rural population.
